newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle landing reset for Friday.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle landing reset for Friday.

text.p: Cloudy skies in Florida forced mission control on Thursday to postpone by 24 hours the planned homecoming of the space shuttle Columbia.
The shuttle's crew of five were minutes away from firing Columbia's braking rockets to begin their descent when flight controllers called off the planned 8:10 a.m. EST (1310 GMT) landing.
"We are going to call it a day ... for trying to get home and we are going to plan for tomorrow," mission control's Curt Brown told the astronauts.

"Give me another day up here and I'll take every second of it," said veteran astronaut Story Musgrave, who is making his sixth and final shuttle flight. At 61, Musgrave is the oldest person to fly in space.

Mission control had briefly flirted with the idea of diverting the shuttle to its backup landing strip in California but eventually decided to reschedule touchdown for 8:01 a.m. EST (1301 GMT) on Friday at Florida's Kennedy Space Centre.

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration prefers to land the shuttle whenever possible at its Florida base to avoid the additional $1 million cost of transporting the shuttle back from California.
The weather in Florida was expected to improve on Friday, contrary to an earlier forecast that had caused NASA to order the shuttle home one day earlier than planned.
The extra day in space will make Columbia's voyage the second longest shuttle flight ever.
The mission, which began Nov. 19, was marred by a jammed airlock hatch that forced NASA to cancel a pair of space walks.

The astronauts released and later retrieved two science satellites. A U.S.-German telescope studied the life cycles of stars and a prototype computer chip factory manufactured ultra-pure semiconductors for the electronics industry.
